doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Personal Katrina damage and rebuilding efforts
summary: Her house was flooded and wind-damaged; she describes displaced colleagues and the musicians' village and Ellis Marsalis Center.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I doubt there was anybody in the city that was not affected by that. Were you personally affected in a dramatic way?

Well not as dramatic as some people. But I did have the flooding to the extent that we had to gut everything, take out all the walls, even the ceiling, the flooring, because of the water, and had wind damage. Part of my roof was in the driveway and all of that. But that’s able to be repaired. It’s the people whose homes floated down the street, whose homes just collapsed, their situation is far worse than mine. Because in my area now I was very glad to see that my neighbors are coming back and working on their homes, that kind of thing. But the biggest thing for me is that I have not been able to get in to my own home while they’re doing the repairs but I do have a place to live. Okay, I have a place to live. And I’m in New Orleans and I’m back at work. We have people who can’t even come back because they don’t have a place to live. They would like to come back and work but there’s no place to live while they work so they’re out there and it’s like they’re stranded. And there are many people like that. And believe me, believe me, they all want to come back home. They all want to come back home. They all want to work. They all want to be a part of this process of bringing New Orleans back. That’s what we’re saying, or rebuilding New Orleans. They all want to be a part of that. But you’ve got to have some place to live while you’re doing it.
I just got a mailing from, I’m not sure, Wynton Marsalis is on a big fundraiser coming up and there’ve been a lot of efforts and I hope that they have positive results for all of you down there.

Yes, yes. Well you know there’s a special thing going on, this Habitat for Humanities is doing a thing for a musician’s village. So they are — and you know that involves sweat equity and all of that kind of thing so that the musicians who are applying, who have applied for a home, they have to come in and do some work, help them in building their homes. So they are about the business of setting up a place so that the musicians can come back. And they’re going to establish a center, an Ellis Marsalis Center in that area for children so that you would teach the children the music. So that’s looking good.
